quote: It's 20, but one's broken. So let's call it nineteen, two hundred and sixty five kilowatt panels.
stewart_read: The orphaned_flow protocol requires asking 'Is your system working?' with broken/not_working as a hard_dq_answer trigger for orphaned handling. The customer discloses a broken panel directly, but the rep never asks the required working-status question or logs whether this affects design/DQ status.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged one broken panel out of 20 as immaterial chit-chat rather than a system-status disclosure worth formally logging.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to run the orphaned_flow question set explicitly whenever a customer discloses an existing system — 'Is your system currently working?' — rather than letting a customer's aside stand in for the qualifying question.

stewart_read: This is a direct, unprompted ask for Tesla Powerwall — Ion's only battery product — volunteered by the customer without any pitch. The rep logs it ('K. Battery backup. Let me get that down.') but never reflects it back as a value anchor for the appointment or callback.
coaching_implication: Show the rep this clip as an example of a gift the customer handed them — next time, reflect it back ('Great, we carry the Tesla Powerwall, that's exactly the kind of add-on the specialist can size for you') to build anticipation instead of just noting it down.

quote: I'm looking to add on to that system. That system is not properly sized for this house.
stewart_read: The customer states her own system is undersized — a strong, self-diagnosed pain point that practically writes the curiosity hook for the rep ('that's exactly why a proper resize matters, let's get the numbers to our specialist'). The rep instead moves straight into a factual follow-up about installer identity without reflecting the sizing problem back.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the call ends in a provisional DQ minutes later, the rep may not have wanted to build anticipation for an appointment that might not happen due to the WASCO utility block.
coaching_implication: Even with DQ risk pending, a brief acknowledgment ('that undersizing issue is a great reason to get this looked at properly') costs nothing and keeps the customer warm for the callback.

quote: I've provided all of this information.
stewart_read: Customer flags redundant data collection, suggesting this may be a recycled or repeat-touch lead where bill/utility info could already be on file. Rep's response addresses the immediate friction (data-pull glitch) but doesn't ask when or with whom the customer previously spoke.
alternative_hypothesis: This is not a vulnerability disclosure (health/loss/financial hardship) under coaching_philosophy.empathy_on_vulnerability_disclosure — it's operational annoyance at redundant intake, a narrower and lower-stakes friction point.
coaching_implication: When a customer signals 'I already gave you this,' a quick acknowledgment plus a note to check the account history protects rapport and avoids the appearance the company doesn't track its own leads.

quote: Do you know who you got installed with originally with
stewart_read: This is the correct orphaned_flow question (installer identity, checking against Sunrun/Pink Solar hard-DQ list) and it's asked appropriately — included here as a positive contrast to the missed 'is it working' question just above.
coaching_implication: This shows the rep knows part of the orphaned_flow script; the gap is completeness, not knowledge — useful framing for the 1-on-1 so it doesn't read as a total protocol miss.

quote: because as of right now, their the utility company is not accepting any solar applications and does not have any plans to reopen their solar program at the at the moment.
stewart_read: This is a clean, honest disqualification delivered with a check-and-verify posture (rep looked it up proactively rather than guessing), and the rep offers a concrete next step (callback after checking with the design team) rather than a dead end.
alternative_hypothesis: A reactive read would call this a lost sale, but the transparency and follow-up commitment support the strategic read — protecting the customer's time and the company's credibility over forcing a doomed appointment.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this as a model for utility-blocked leads: verify first, be transparent, commit to a specific next action rather than vague deflection.

quote: So I'll I'll I'll message them right now, and then I'll give you a callback with an update later. Does that work for you?
stewart_read: The callback commitment has no specific day or time attached — 'later' is not a locked appointment mechanic. Even in a provisional-DQ scenario, a concrete callback window protects the lead from going cold.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the DQ depends on the design team's answer (unknown timing), an exact time may not have been available to promise.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to anchor even provisional callbacks to a specific day/timeframe ('I'll have an answer by end of day tomorrow and will call you then') rather than open-ended 'later.'

quote: Do you want this info anyway?
stewart_read: Rep offers to still walk the customer through information despite the likely DQ, then reverses and declines to take more of her time — shows good instinct not to force a pitch on a dead-end lead, though the offer itself was slightly muddled.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as indecision rather than a deliberate customer-time-protection move, since the rep asks then immediately answers for the customer.
coaching_implication: Minor: encourage clean, single-take decisions on this kind of judgment call rather than asking then answering own question.
